summary: Defines the AES-XCBC-MAC-96 message authentication algorithm and how it is used with IPsec. It builds on the CBC-MAC idea, which is secure only for messages of one fixed length, and extends it to handle messages of any length. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: A tamper-proof seal on a message shows nobody changed it. This memo defines a seal made with a well-known scrambling method that works for messages of any size, and says how to use it in IPsec.

questions: why is cbc-mac not secure for variable length messages
how does xcbc-mac use three keys
how long is the aes-xcbc-mac-96 authenticator
subtitle: A message authentication code built from AES that stays secure for messages of any length, for use with IPsec ESP and AH.

tldr.problem: Classic CBC-MAC is secure only for messages of one pre-selected fixed length, but IPsec datagrams vary in length, so it is not suitable.
tldr.mechanism: AES-XCBC-MAC-96 derives three keys from one 128-bit key, chains AES over the message blocks with the first key, uses the second or third key on the last block depending on whether it is full, and keeps the leftmost 96 bits.
tldr.outcome: It gives IPsec ESP and AH an AES-based authenticator for arbitrary-length datagrams, with performance equivalent to classic CBC-MAC.

today: RFC 3566 is a Proposed Standard from September 2003, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Basic CBC-MAC Falls Short
sections.content:
A Message Authentication Code (MAC) is a key-dependent one way hash function. It provides data integrity and data origin authentication, and these hold only as widely as the secret key is shared. A popular construction runs a block cipher in Cipher Block Chaining (CBC) mode.

The basic CBC-MAC appends a single 1 bit and then enough 0 bits to fill a block, splits the message into b-bit blocks, and chains them: each block is XORed with the previous result and then encrypted. The last result is the authenticator.

This is secure only for messages up to a pre-selected fixed length. The RFC rejects it for IPsec for two reasons. An IPsec authenticator must handle messages of arbitrary length, and padding short messages up to the fixed length may need extra encryption operations, an unacceptable computational penalty.
sections.plainLanguage: The old method is like a stamp machine built for one exact paper size. Longer papers are not safe, and shrinking everything to fit wastes time.

sections.title: The AES-XCBC-MAC-96 Algorithm
sections.content:
AES-XCBC-MAC-96 is a variant of basic CBC-MAC that is secure for messages of arbitrary length. All the encryption MUST use AES with a 128-bit key. Given a secret key K and a message of n blocks, where the last block is 1 to 128 bits:

  • Derive three 128-bit keys by encrypting the constants 0x0101...01, 0x0202...02 and 0x0303...03 with K, giving K1, K2 and K3.
  • Start with E[0] as all zeros. For each block before the last, XOR it with the previous result and encrypt with K1.
  • If the last block is a full 128 bits, XOR it with the previous result and K2, then encrypt with K1.
  • If it is shorter, pad it with a single 1 bit and then 0 bits, XOR with the previous result and K3, then encrypt with K1.
  • The authenticator is the leftmost 96 bits of the final 128-bit result.

An empty message is padded and encrypted as in the short-block case. This never happens for ESP or AH. For verification, the full 128-bit value is computed and the first 96 bits are compared with the authenticator field.
sections.plainLanguage: The method makes three secret helper keys from one key. It scrambles the message piece by piece, uses a different finishing touch depending on whether the last piece was full, and keeps only part of the result as the seal.

sections.title: Keys, Padding and Truncation
sections.content:
AES-XCBC-MAC-96 is a secret key algorithm. For ESP or AH, a fixed key length of 128 bits MUST be supported and other lengths MUST NOT be supported. It needs 384 bits of keying material (128 bits for the AES key plus two times the block size), which is generated from the single 128-bit key. Three keys are used so the length of the input does not need to be known in advance, which helps systems that assemble large packets in one pass.

A strong pseudo-random function MUST be used to generate the 128-bit key. That key and K1, K2 and K3 should be used for nothing else, since reuse in another cryptographic setting would invalidate the security of the authentication. No weak keys were known at the time of writing, and if any are identified they MUST be rejected. Periodic key refreshment is advised.

No extra padding is needed beyond what the algorithm does, and no implicit packet padding is required for AH. The 128-bit result is truncated to the first 96 bits, which MUST be supported. No other lengths are supported. 96 bits was chosen because it is the default authenticator length in AH.
sections.plainLanguage: The secret key is for this job only, like a key that opens one door and nothing else. The final seal is cut down to a fixed length so every sender and receiver agrees on its size.

sections.title: Performance and Interaction with ESP
sections.content:
The main cost of any CBC MAC variant is the underlying block cipher. AES-XCBC-MAC-96 uses a minimum number of AES calls, one for each block of the message or fraction of a block, so its performance is equivalent to classic CBC-MAC. Key expansion needs 3 additional AES encryptions, which can be done once in advance for each secret key.

At the time of writing, the RFC knows of no issues that stop AES-XCBC-MAC-96 being used with any particular ESP cipher algorithm.
sections.plainLanguage: The new method is just as fast as the old one. The only extra work is making the three helper keys, and that is done once.

sections.title: Test Vectors
sections.content: The RFC lists seven test cases, provided by John Black, co-author of the XCBC-MAC algorithm, and checked with two independent implementations. All use the key 000102030405060708090a0b0c0d0e0f with inputs of 0, 3, 16, 20, 32, 34 and 1000 bytes. Each case gives the full 128-bit AES-XCBC-MAC value and its 96-bit truncation, so implementers can check their code.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo includes practice questions with the right answers so builders can check their work.

sections.title: Security and IANA Considerations
sections.content:
The security of AES-XCBC-MAC-96 rests on the strength of AES. At the time of writing, no practical cryptographic attacks were known against AES or AES-XCBC-MAC-96. Strength also depends on a correct implementation, secure key management, the strength of the secret key and correct implementations on all participating systems. The test vectors are there to help verify code.

IANA assigned AH Transform Identifier 9 to AH_AES-XCBC-MAC and AH/ESP Authentication Algorithm Value 9 to AES-XCBC-MAC.
sections.plainLanguage: The seal is only as good as the lock it is built from and how carefully people use it. Official number 9 was reserved for it in the IPsec lists.

viz.caption: THE THREE DERIVED KEYS AND THEIR JOBS

items.title: K1
items.text: Encrypts every block in the chain, including the last.

items.title: K2
items.text: XORed into the last block when it is a full 128 bits.

items.title: K3
items.text: XORed into the last block when it is shorter and has been padded.
